summary: Round 3, test-reviewer lane (testability the rows prescribe; no code, no tests in this diff). All three round-2 minors are fixed in the sense they were raised: the no-op dedup now dies on an offsets assertion, the M4.10c anchor now demands a commit the last checkpoint did not cover, and the order assertion is sent to the tier that can detect a deleted sort. Every factual claim the fixes added was re-verified against the tree (Checkpoint MAGIC/VERSION/decode-refuses, the LinkedHashMap order-preserving copy at Checkpoint.java:81-82, CheckpointWriterContentTest's everyDeltas=1 takeover fixture, GoldenCheckpointTest's three tests and its measured delete-the-sort record, CheckpointTest's two order tests, SegmentKey.render, DefaultIngest:349 and :356-360, Sequencer:77-89) and all of them hold. Four minors remain, three of them surviving mutations against the round-2 fixes themselves -- one is a NEW mutation of the kind round 2 found (the returned OFFSETS are still unpinned), one is a residue the T2 fix narrowed but did not close, and one is the T3 fix OVERSHOOTING and disarming the only detector the tree has for a different mutation. None blocks: each is one clause of prose, and per the round rules fixing a minor is permitted and usually wrong.
verified_from_round_2: T1 (no-op dedup -- record, checkpoint, recover, never consult) -- ADDRESSED AND SUFFICIENT FOR THE MUTATION AS RAISED. backlog-notes.md:301-307 names the mutation verbatim and states the killing assertion is on the OFFSETS: a replayed (podId, flushSeq) must leave nextOffset UNCHANGED. Under the no-op the replay commits afresh and the sequencer's nextOffset advances a second time, so the prescribed assertion fails. The clause also says why the earlier guidance could not see it ('nothing about which key comes back can see this'), which is the part that stops the next implementer re-deriving the key-shaped test. backlog.md:125 carries the short form ('Offsets must not advance twice -- a dedup that records and never CONSULTS passes everything else'), so a session that reads only the row still gets it. The assertion is on behaviour (offsets a producer would receive), not on the presence of a field or a call, so it does not restate the implementation.

T2 (the prescribed anchor was green with no format change, because CheckpointWriterContentTest runs everyDeltas=1 and poda->42 is already checkpointed before the takeover) -- ADDRESSED, PARTIALLY. backlog-notes.md:256-262 states the mechanism accurately (verified: CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:143 builds the first writer with everyDeltas=1 and :144-145 commits poda 42 and asserts it reached a written checkpoint; CheckpointCursor.java:74-79 gives the successor a checkpoint-sourced path to that map without any format change) and now requires a commit AFTER the last checkpoint and before the takeover. That does defeat the checkpoint-only recovery mutation FOR A FIXTURE THAT PUTS THE ASSERTED VALUE IN THAT COMMIT -- but the row does not say the asserted value must come from it. See finding T5.

T3 (the order assertion was sent to the tier measured not to detect delete-the-sort) -- ADDRESSED, AND OVERSHOT. backlog-notes.md:265-271 now forbids the golden test and names CheckpointTest's order tests as the detectors. Verified: CheckpointTest.theENCODERSortsWhateverOrderTheCallerHandedIn inserts descending and reads the ENCODED order, so it fails deterministically on a deleted sort, and GoldenCheckpointTest.java:25-29 does record the measured green result the row cites. But the same javadoc, :31-35, records a SECOND measured result the fix does not mention, and the blanket 'NOT in the golden test' disarms it. See finding T6.

P6/P7/P8/P9 (production lane, round 2) -- not my lane, but the two mechanisms are now stated separately at backlog-notes.md:246-263 and the 'cannot express a qualified key' overclaim is now parenthesised as 'the point is agreement, not impossibility', both of which are consistent with the code I read (Checkpoint.java:42-49, :147-152). The 'hand-built golden' misattribution at :253-255 is corrected to 'generated once from the encoder and verified by hand', which is what GoldenCheckpointTest.java:15-23 actually says.
claims_verified_in_baselines_review_txt: 'M4.10d's discriminator was a takeover when the defect is a POD RESTART, so dedup on the bare pair passed it' -- ACCURATE. Matches the round-1 test-reviewer major verbatim in substance, and the mechanism holds: a cross-leader fixture has one incarnation of poda, so whatever is durable never varies.

'Skip-and-return satisfied refuse while turning a landed flush into a producer-visible failure' -- ACCURATE, and re-checked against the code rather than against the earlier finding: Sequencer.java:77-89 defines the return as what a caller matches by its submitted segment key, and DefaultIngest.java:356-360 completes the append exceptionally with 'the commit did not carry the stream this append wrote' when the run is absent.

'AND THE PRESCRIPTIONS STILL ADMITTED A NO-OP: record lastAppliedFlushSeq, checkpoint it, recover it, never consult it -- every named mutation killed ... The assertion that catches it is on the OFFSETS, and every piece of guidance I had written pointed at the returned key instead' -- ACCURATE. It describes the round-2 T1 finding correctly, including the self-attribution ('guidance I had written'), and does not overstate it as a major.

'the chain ALREADY carries a restart-surviving token (SegmentKey: timestampMillis, podShortId, per-pod sequence)' -- ACCURATE as a description of the components: SegmentKey.java:166 renders '%s/data/%s/%019d-%s-%016x-h%d-%s.bseg' in exactly that order, and SegmentPublisher.java:136-138 is the 'unique WITHOUT coordination' comment. The hedge 'may void the whole row' is correct -- whether the token is genuinely restart-surviving is M4.10b's ADR to argue, and the row asks it to.
'THE THING BEING SPLIT IS THE SPLIT ... splitting it further means one row per commit' -- consistent with the diff, which is three documentation files and no code.

'there were six across the two roles at round 1' -- the six MAJORS is right (3 reviewer + 3 test-reviewer at acf50ad67afe). But the sentence attributes the count to 'EVERY FINDING', and there were eleven findings at round 1 (6 major, 5 minor). See finding T7.

findings.title: The T1 fix pins the GLOBAL offsets and the RETURNED KEY, but never that the returned delta carries the ORIGINAL attempt's offsets -- so a refusal that answers the retry with fresh offsets survives every prescription
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: on a replayed (podId, flushSeq), do not append and do not advance anything -- but build the returned CommitDelta from the CURRENT state: one SegmentCommit carrying request.segmentKey(), with each run's firstOffset set to the stream's current nextOffset (or 0). Walk every prescription in M4.10d as it now stands. (a) ':285-295, the retrying caller gets the ORIGINAL segment key back' -- green, the key returned IS request.segmentKey(), which is by construction the original one; the row's own T1 clause at :304 concedes this is unobservable. (b) ':306, a replayed pair must leave nextOffset UNCHANGED' -- green, nothing was appended and no offset advanced; this assertion is on the SEQUENCER's state, not on the reply. (c) ':275-283, restarted pod reissuing 0 for a NEW segment is ACCEPTED' -- green, unaffected. (d) '< for <=' -- green, the exact-equal replay is the case being refused. (e) 'per-pod map, not a fleet-wide long' -- green. (f) 'survives a takeover' -- green, and this is where the mutation is FORCED rather than chosen: the durable window M4.10c prescribes is Checkpoint's Map<String, Long> pods (Checkpoint.java:42-44), a podId to a bare long. It records enough to DETECT a replay and nothing to ANSWER one. After the newest checkpoint has covered the original commit -- 'the case where the replay arrives after a checkpoint recorded it', which is the parent M4.10 row's headline and M4.10d's own opening line at :277 -- the original firstOffsets are not recoverable at all, so an implementer who has satisfied every stated criterion must invent offsets or return none. WHAT SHIPS: the retrying producer's appends complete successfully with offsets that the sequencer will hand to the NEXT commit, so two disjoint sets of records claim one offset range -- the 'silent duplication that _id dedup would mask inconsistently' from the parent row, arriving through the fix for it. THE MISSING CLAUSE: the refusal must return the SAME offsets the first attempt returned, asserted by capturing the first delta's firstOffset per run and requiring the replay's delta to equal it -- and, because that is not derivable from a long, M4.10b's 'THE OUTPUT IS A LIST OF FORMATS' at :212-216 has to decide what the durable window carries to ANSWER a retry, not only to detect one. NOTE ALSO that this undercuts the sentence added this round at :185-187, 'M4.10d is blocked by M4.10b -- not by M4.10c, whose outcome it survives either way': if the answer must survive a checkpoint boundary, M4.10d's contract depends on what M4.10c made durable, either way it goes.

findings.title: The T2 fix requires A commit after the last checkpoint, not that the ASSERTED value comes from it, so checkpoint-only recovery still passes the anchor
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION (the same one T2 named, narrowed but not closed): leave CommitDelta UNCHANGED and seed CheckpointWriter's pods from the recovered CHECKPOINT alone. Build the fixture to the letter of :259-262 -- everyDeltas = 2; commit(poda, 42); commit(podb, 7) triggers a checkpoint carrying {poda: 42, podb: 7}; commit(podb, 8) is the required 'commit after the last checkpoint and before the takeover'; takeover; assert the successor's first checkpoint carries poda -> 42. Green with no format change, because poda -> 42 came from the checkpoint and the uncheckpointed delta carried only podb. The row's criterion is satisfied and its purpose -- proving the DELTA carries the window -- is not. THE MISSING CLAUSE: the asserted pod's value must be one no checkpoint before the takeover ever held; i.e. commit poda 42 AFTER the last checkpoint, or check a value that differs from the checkpointed one (poda -> 41 checkpointed, poda -> 42 only on the chain, assert 42). SECOND, SMALLER GAP IN THE SAME CLAUSE: as written the prescription is unsatisfiable without a change the row does not name -- at everyDeltas = 1 (CheckpointWriter.java:87, CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:143) EVERY commit is immediately checkpointed, so no commit can be 'after the last checkpoint' until the fixture also raises everyDeltas. Derivable, but the row diagnoses everyDeltas = 1 and then does not say to move it.

findings.title: The T3 fix overshoots: 'pin its ORDER too -- but NOT in the golden test' disarms the only detector this tree has for the record's order-preserving copy, which the cited javadoc records as MEASURED two paragraphs below the sentence it quotes
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, if M4.10c's new field is a keyed collection: substitute Map.copyOf for the order-preserving LinkedHashMap copy in the Checkpoint record's compact constructor (Checkpoint.java:81-82) for that field. Walk the tier the row now sends the order assertion to. CheckpointTest.theENCODERSortsWhateverOrderTheCallerHandedIn encodes a fixture and reads the ENCODED order -- the encoder sorts explicitly, so the emitted order is ascending whatever the record's map did with it: GREEN. twoCheckpointsDifferingONLYInInsertionOrderEncodeIdentically: green for the same reason. everyFieldSurvivesARoundTrip compares with Map.equals, which is order-insensitive: green. The mutation is caught ONLY by a test that decodes committed bytes and reads the keys back in file order -- GoldenCheckpointTest.theGoldenBytesCarryStreamsAndPodsInASCENDINGOrder, whose own javadoc at GoldenCheckpointTest.java:31-35 records exactly this, measured: 'substituting Map.copyOf for the LinkedHashMap copy fails theGoldenBytesCarryStreamsAndPodsInASCENDINGOrder in 6 of 6 fresh runs. Reading committed bytes makes it the more robust of the two order detectors, not the weaker one.' Checkpoint.java:72-74 says the same thing from the production side. So the fix quotes lines 25-29 of that javadoc and contradicts lines 31-35 of it. An implementer who follows :268 literally adds no order assertion to the new golden's test, and the new field's copy semantics go unconstrained. THE ACCURATE FORM: the ENCODER-SORT assertion belongs in the codec test (CheckpointTest) because the golden cannot see a deleted sort; the golden test still pins the RECORD's order-preserving copy, which the codec test cannot see. Two mutations, two tiers -- the current sentence collapses them into one and drops the second.

findings.title: 'EVERY FINDING was a row admitting a wrong implementation ... and there were six across the two roles at round 1' -- there were eleven findings; six were majors
findings.failure_scenario: Counted from the records the packet points at: .harness/review/acf50ad67afe...reviewer.json carries 3 major (P1, P2, P3) and 2 minor (P4, P5); .harness/review/acf50ad67afe...test-reviewer.json carries 3 major and 3 minor. Six is the MAJOR count, and every one of the five minors is also a row admitting something wrong (P4 prescribes a header-version bump where the format's mechanism is a new kind; P5 says M4.10c's stated scope does not fix the symptom it cites; the test-lane minors are the golden order tier, the absent production replay path, and a census sentence the fifth golden falsifies). So under the sentence's own predicate the number is eleven. Reported because this is the file whose entire function is an honest record, and because the M0.76 entry three lines above is an essay about four numbers that were not what they claimed. Not blocking: the figure is right for the class it most plausibly means, and the enumeration that follows it names five findings rather than six, so no reader is misled about which findings there were.

not_findings_but_worth_the_commit_body: The M4.10c anchor prescribes inverting doesNotContainKey("poda") to assert poda -> 42, while the same row says the checkpoint key may become qualified ('e7:poda', :246-249). If the ADR qualifies the key, the literal assertion is wrong. Not a finding: it fails loudly rather than passing vacuously, so the implementer adapts it rather than shipping past it.

M4.10d:308-312 already says plainly that no production caller replays a pair today and that the row must either add the retry path or state that its coverage stops at the sequencer seam. That is the right disclosure and it is what keeps the T4 assertion honest about what tier it can live in.
The three round-2 fixes are all ADDITIVE prose; nothing in this diff weakens or deletes a prescription, and no assertion anywhere in the tree was loosened alongside it (no test file is staged).
